name: Beer brewing, Late Uruk Godin Tepe, central Zagros
summary: Beer identified from oxalate residue on a Late Uruk ceramic sherd at Godin Tepe in Iran, the earliest reported chemical identification of beer in the Middle East.
description: Oxalate ions on a Late Uruk ceramic sherd from Godin Tepe, in the Kangavar valley of the central Zagros, are the basis of the earliest reported identification of beer in the Middle East. Encyclopaedia Iranica dates the late Uruk period, to which the pottery of Godin's Period V enclosure is compared, to about 3500-3200 BCE, and says the enclosure is assumed to have been occupied by Sumerian or Elamite traders.

impact.note: Scored for what is evidenced here, beer in one Late Uruk trading community (reach 1): the wider Mesopotamian beer tradition is not shown to descend from it and is not sourced on this card; beer was a new way of turning grain into a storable drink (depth 2), with later brewing in the region as its few successors (generativity 1).

date.label: late Uruk period, ca. 3500–3200 BCE
date.basis: As the cited source gives it.

events.statement: Beer was identified from oxalate ions on a Late Uruk ceramic sherd from Godin Tepe. The years are not in the quoted sentence: they are Encyclopaedia Iranica's date for the late Uruk period (ca. 3500-3200 B.C.E., the second source), and the sherd itself is not separately dated here.

evidence.supports: The earliest reported identification of beer in the Middle East, for example, is based on a positive identification of oxalate ions on a Late Uruk ceramic sherd from Godin Tepe in Iran
evidence.locator: Introduction, paragraph on chemical markers of beer in ceramics

earliest_record.rationale: The earliest dated evidence found for this capability in this community. No review has yet confirmed that nothing earlier exists.

unresolved.note: Paskulin cites Michel, McGovern and Badler 1993, 'The first wine and beer: chemical detection of ancient fermented beverages', for the identification; neither that paper nor the same authors' 1992 letter 'Chemical evidence for ancient beer' (Nature 360, 24) was read, so the sherd's findspot, level (Period V?) and own date, and whether the beer was of barley, remain to be taken from them.

Beer brewing in lowland Mesopotamia (Late Uruk texts, later rations and depictions) is the larger capability the lead named; it is not sourced on this card and needs its own research before it is scored.

Raqefet Cave (claimed cereal brewing around 11,000 BCE) and Hierakonpolis (predynastic Egyptian brewery) are separate communities and need their own records; the Chinese fermented drink at Jiahu was not compared.

research.note: Paskulin and colleagues call the Godin Tepe sherd the earliest reported identification of beer in the Middle East and make no claim of independence; Encyclopaedia Iranica says the Period V enclosure is assumed to have been occupied by Sumerian or Elamite traders, so the brewing may have come with lowland people, and the question is open.
